newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks seen opening mixed to higher.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks seen opening mixed to higher.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open mixed to higher on Wednesday, but analysts say it is unclear what direction the market will take later in the session after a three-day streak of record highs.

"I don't see anything that stands in the way of it going higher," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood. "It looks like we are going to have another reasonably good day if we can get technology stocks turned around."
On Tuesday the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed past 7500, gaining 61 points to close at 7539.
The technology-laden Nasdaq slipped under pressure from networking stocks and semiconductor equipment companies. The Nasdaq composite closed down about 10.33 points at 1401.71.
In early-morning activity the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was up 5/32 at a 6.83 percent yield.
The Standard & Poor's futures index was off 0.60 to 868.10.

Hildegard Zagorski, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said the lower futures number may signal a mixed or even lower opening. But she added, "Given the strong showing of the Dow yesterday, we probably will open higher."
Analysts said they would be watching technology stocks, after networking and semiconductor equipment stocks came under pressure Tuesday.

They said tobacco stocks such as Dow component Philip Morris Cos Inc may show signs of weakness following news that Brown & Williamson has had broken ranks with other cigarette makers in the tobacco settlement talks.

Japan's Nikkei average closed down 242.62 points, or 1.18 percent, at 20,289.93. In London the FTSE 100 was off 9.2 points at 4730.4. U.S. stocks trading in London were lower after the third straight day of record runs.

The dollar fell against the yen in Tokyo after comments by U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers raised concerns over Japan's trade surplus ahead of the G7 summit later this month. The dollar was trading at 111.20/25 yen. In Europe the dollar was trading at 1.7160/70 marks.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that stock options have enriched thousands of corporate executives in this 6-1/2-year-old bull market, but it's a different story for companies whose shares have plunged.
The New York Times said in its Market Place column that tax writers see potential government revenue in the airlines.
